rings.label: Ring 1 — device farm
rings.note: A GROUP BY on device_id with HAVING COUNT(*) > 3 finds this. Included as the baseline.

rings.label: Ring 2 — mule payout
rings.signature: 9 accounts paying out to 3 bank accounts
rings.note: Also rule-catchable. Establishes that the strong signal weighting works.

rings.label: Ring 3 — the chain
rings.signature: A-B-C-D-E, each adjacent pair sharing exactly one identifier, ends sharing nothing
rings.note: THE HEADLINE. A and E have zero identifiers in common. Only a multi-hop traversal joins them.

rings.label: Ring 4 — circular transfers
rings.signature: 6 accounts, three overlapping money loops of 3, 4 and 5 legs
rings.note: Shares NO identifiers. Detected purely from cycles in TRANSFERRED. No clean SQL equivalent exists.

rings.label: Ring 5 — address variants
rings.signature: 7 accounts at one doorway, written seven different ways
rings.note: Seven distinct raw strings collapse to one :Address node. Without normalisation, seven unrelated accounts.

rings.label: Ring 6 — dormant bust-out
rings.signature: 10 accounts quiet for six weeks, then all draw their full limit within 72 hours
rings.note: Shares 3 devices (weak, forms the component) plus a co-timed drawdown (strong scoring signal).

noise.label: Families sharing an address
noise.note: 60 households of 2-4 accounts. Small, single weak link type, no transfers. Should score low.

noise.label: College WiFi IP (40 accounts)
noise.note: Degree 40, above MAX_IDENTIFIER_DEGREE. Proves the super-node cutoff both removes noise and bounds cost.

noise.label: Office IP (12 accounts)
noise.note: Under the cap, so it forms a real cluster -- but LOGGED_IN_FROM is weighted 0.15, so it scores low.

noise.label: Married couples sharing a bank account
noise.note: PAYS_OUT_TO is the strongest signal, but a pair of 2 is below MIN_RING_SIZE, so it never becomes a ring.
